title: What If You Used 100% of Your Brain?

shots.line: Your alarm hasn't rung yet, you're already awake.
You hear everything.
The fridge humming, a pipe knocking in the wall, a cat three floors down, sneezing.
You open your history book, one glance, twelve pages, done.
Your mom walks in, talking fast, milk, eggs, rice, soap, and that blue cheese you hate.
You don't write it down, you don't need to.
You remember every word, and the order she said them in.
Mom stares at you.
Max, since when do you listen?
You just smile.
At school, a teacher asks a question nobody can answer.
You've answered it before he finishes asking.
Leo leans over. Dude, what are you?
You shrug. You just notice things.
The clock, the crack in the board, the way your teacher blinks when he lies about homework.
At lunch, a tray slides off a table.
You see it coming, you catch it.
Without even looking.
The whole cafeteria turns.
Somebody whispers. Did he just know?
Yes, you did.
After school, you walk home.
You count the cars. 41.
You count the pigeons. 9.
You count your steps. 600.
You even count the freckles on the bus driver's neck.
Don't ask.
And back at your place, your toast hasn't even popped and you already know it'll burn.
Three weeks ago, none of this existed.
You were normal.
Most people can hold about four things in mind at once. You were one of them.
Then, a man in a gray coat stopped you outside school.
Mr. Black, free trial.
One headband, 20 minutes a day.
He said it was tested. Safe. Approved.
He never showed you a single paper.
Then he pointed at a tiny red switch.
Burst. Emergencies only.
One use. Then the band dies.
You nodded. You never planned to touch it.
He smiled. You know the old story.
We only use 10 % of our brain. Imagine the other 90. Waiting. Locked away.
You laughed.
Then you put it on.
Now you hold 40 things at once. Forty.
A normal brain runs on about 20 watts. About as much as a dim light bulb. Yours runs on 60.
A normal brain has about 86 billion neurons. Yours fire all of them.
And here's the rule. Your brain got louder. Your body did not. Same stomach. Same blood. Same legs.
You can think a thousand thoughts. You can only do one thing.
And every thought burns fuel.
A normal brain is 2 % of your weight. Yet it eats 20 % of your energy.
Yours eats much, much more. Think big and you burn fast.
So what if your brain used 100 % of its capacity?
Day one. Plus, a normal adult reads about 250 words a minute.
You finish a whole novel on the bus.
The catch? You notice every typo. Every single one.
Your teacher hands you her essay.
You hand it back with six pages of notes.
Day two. Math test. 40 minutes. You finish in nine.
Your teacher stares at your paper. Then at you.
Max. Did you cheat?
Ask me anything.
He does. You answer before he finishes.
Plus, a perfect score.
Minus, he makes you retake it.
Alone. In his office.
Day three. Leo drops his phone off the balcony.
You don't think. You just catch it. Two fingers. Leo screens.
How? How did you do that?
A normal person reacts in about a quarter of a second. You? A blink before that.
Day four. A normal person needs months to learn a new language. You need six days.
You order lunch in Spanish.
The waiter answers in Spanish. You answer faster. He gets lost.
His grandma applauds.
Day five. The supermarket cashier scans your mom's cart.
You glance at the screen. Wrong price. Two coins too many.
Mom pays less.
The cashier blushes.
Mom tells everyone.
Day six. A strong chess player looks about six moves ahead.
You look 20.
You beat the school champion in 11 moves.
He asks for a rematch.
You win again while eating a sandwich.
Day seven. You remember every face you've ever seen.
The bus driver from third grade. The lady at the pharmacy. A boy you passed once at the airport.
You say hello to all of them.
Plus, people feel special.
Minus, people feel watched.
Day eight. Basketball. You see everything.
Where the ball will land. Who will pass. Who will slip.
Plus, you know the perfect shot.
Minus, your arms are still a teenager's.
The ball hits the rim.
Leo winces. Man.
You solved it. And still missed.
Day nine. Leo shows you his math homework.
14 problems. You solve them out loud while brushing your teeth.
Leo copies nothing. He just watches.
Then he sighs. Man. I wish I had a brain like that.
You smile. You don't answer.
Day ten. You try a strategy game. One night. By morning, you're ranked among the best players in the world.
A pro team emails. Then another.
Leo reads over your shoulder. Dude, they're offering you a car!
Day eleven. A memory contest at the school fair.
A normal person remembers about seven digits in a row. You remember 400.
The judge runs out of numbers. He starts reading license plates.
The crowd chants your name.
You hear every voice. Every single one.
Your hands shake.
Day twelve. Your piano teacher plays a song once. Just once.
You play it back. Both hands. Perfect.
She drops her pencil.
It took her three months. It took you 40 seconds.
Day thirteen. You draw your whole city on a wall. Every street. Every shop sign.
People walk past and find their own front doors.
A woman cries. It's her old house. Long gone.
Day fourteen. Your dad's tax form. You find three mistakes in 90 seconds.
He saves a month's rent.
He hugs you. He smells like coffee.
Day fifteen. You fix the school Wi -Fi in six minutes.
The tech guy sits down. He doesn't speak for a while.
Minus. The noise.
A normal brain filters out most of the world.
Yours doesn't.
A hundred voices. A hundred forks. A hundred things you can't stop hearing.
By noon, your head pounds.
By three, you wear earplugs.
By dinner, two pairs.
Minus. Sleep.
A teenager needs about eight hours. You get four.
And you dream in spreadsheets.
And then there's the hunger.
A normal brain burns about 120 grams of sugar a day. Yours burns almost 400.
Your mom opens the fridge. Empty.
Max.
That's your fifth bowl of rice.
Mom, it's my brain's fifth bowl.
Sprinters know another rule.
React faster than a tenth of a second and the judges decide you must have guessed. It's called a false start.
You test it. Your brain shouts, go!
Your legs say, wait!
You can see the gun. You just can't beat it.
Plus, you never false start.
Minus, you never win.
But where it gets really crazy is week three.
A city asks you to fix its bus routes. You redraw them over one weekend. Waiting time drops.
A million people ride faster.
Nobody knows your name.
Then you write a short proof for a problem that stumped professors for years.
You post it online. By morning, three universities email you. One offers a full scholarship.
By lunch, a TV crew stands outside your house.
The headline, teen genius breaks math.
Your mom cries.
Your dad prints it and frames it.
Your grandma sees it on the news. She asks only one thing.
Did you eat?
And one evening, Mr. Black knocks on your door.
Same gray coat. Same smile.
Max! You're famous! We want a thousand more of you.
A big launch. A big stage. And you? You're our face.
Your stomach drops. You can't say why. Not yet.
And there's a cost. A cost nobody talks about.
Boredom.
You know every plot twist before the movie says it.
You know the next note in every song.
You know how every joke ends.
Here's why. Dopamine. Those brain cells fire hardest when something is better than expected. A surprise.
In 1997, a team led by Wolfram Schultz showed it.
The cells didn't care about the reward. They cared about the surprise.
So what happens to a brain that predicts everything? It never gets a surprise.
And it never feels… the spark.
You laugh anyway. You smile on cue.
But inside, it's quiet. Like a song on mute.
At 3am, your mom finds you staring at the ceiling.
Max, you okay?
You say yes. She doesn't believe you.
She makes toast. You both listen to it pop.
Nothing surprises you. Not even her love.
That's the worst part.
Then comes the loneliness. Kids stop sitting with you.
They say you're scary. You hear them say it. You hear everything.
So you start to hide. You miss questions on purpose.
You fail a quiz on Friday.
Hiding who you are costs something too.
Then comes the headache.
The band gets warm. Then hot. Hotter every day.
You visit Dr. Lee, a neurologist near your school.
She scans your head.
Then she frowns.
Max, that old story is wrong. You never use 10%.
Scans show activity all over the brain, even when you sleep.
This band didn't unlock a locked room. It turned the volume up on everything.
And you can't run a furnace on empty.
Is that dangerous?
She doesn't answer.
She taps the scan. See this? Sugar. Your brain is drinking your blood dry.
Let the level fall too low and the brain shuts down. Fainting. Seizures. Worse.
The band pushes harder every day.
She looks you in the eye. Take it off. Tonight.
You nod. You don't. Not yet.
Because everybody finally sees you. Because it feels amazing.
And awful. Usually both at once.
There's one person who doesn't care how smart you are.
Leo. Your best friend since you were 6.
Terrible haircut. Worst jokes.
And a secret knock. Too fast. One slow. Every night he taps it on your window.
You open. He climbs in.
He tells you a joke so bad it hurts.
What do you call a bear with no teeth? A gummy bear.
You groan. You always groan.
Every Friday since 3rd grade you split a cheese sandwich. No crusts.
His rule. Your rule now.
But lately something is off.
You know the punchline before he breathes in. You know his jokes. His moods. His next word.
10 years of data.
So you laugh half a second late.
Leo notices. Dude! You laughed late.
I'm fine.
You're not.
He frowns. Then he grins. Whatever you are now, you're still my idiot.
That night he falls asleep on your floor. Like always. Sneakers on. Mouth open.
You listen to him breathe. Slow. Safe.
Out of every sound in the world, it's the only one that doesn't hurt.
You think about throwing the band away.
Then your phone lights up. Another university. Another offer.
You put the phone face down.
Then one morning he asks the question you were afraid of.
Can I try the band? If you can do it, why can't I?
You hesitate.
40 students already wear it. Hundreds more are waiting.
You say the words. It's safe.
Is it? You don't know. You say it anyway.
Leo whoops.
He starts the next day.
Within a week, he forgets lunch twice.
He gets dizzy on the stairs.
He says he's fine.
You hear his heartbeat race.
The night before launch, you go to the rehearsal.
Mr. Black leaves his laptop open.
You don't mean to look. You can't not look.
A table. 41 names. 6 cells marked red. Next to each one, the same word. Hospital.
And a note. Do not tell parents.
Your blood runs cold.
You copy every row in your head. Names, dates, all of it.
You lie awake that night. Four hours.
Your brain hums. And you feel something you can't predict. Dread.
Launch day.
A packed hall. A thousand people inside. Two hundred thousand more online.
A giant screen hangs 20 meters above the stage. Eight projectors.
Bright. Heavy.
Mr. Black walks out. Arms wide.
Ladies and gentlemen, the future!
You sit in the front row.
Leo grins at you on the way to the stage. Wave at me, okay?
You promise.
Leo stands on stage with the trial students.
The lights are hot.
Leo sways. He grins at you. He waves.
Then, his hand drops.
His knees fold. His eyes roll back. He hits the floor.
His brain burned through everything he ate.
And above him, a tiny click. A bolt in the ceiling.
Nobody hears it.
You do.
Time doesn't slow. You do.
Your brain hands you everything at once.
The rig was built for four projectors. It carries eight.
The bolt is stretching. The cable is shaking.
The screen is coming down.
A screen falling from 20 meters takes two seconds.
Leo is 18 meters from you. A fit teenager runs about 6 meters per second. 18 meters means three seconds. You have two.
Your brain runs 40 plans in a heartbeat. 39 and the same way. The 40th needs a miracle.
You start moving the instant you hear the click.
That buys you half a second. Still short. Half a second short.
That's the rule. Your brain sees the answer. Your legs can't read it. Your legs can't go faster. They can only start earlier.
And you did. And it isn't enough.
Around you, a thousand heads turn. A thousand mouths open. Nobody has moved yet.
You shout his name.
Sound crosses 18 meters in about 500ths of a second. Fast.
Leo doesn't move. He can't hear you. He can't hear anyone.
The shadow of the screen grows over him. 1 .8 seconds. 1 .5.
Leo's lips are gray. His hand is open like he's still waving.
And your own tank is nearly dry. Your hands tremble. Your vision narrows.
Then you remember.
The red switch. Burst. Emergencies only. One use.
Your muscles fire straight from the band. Nine meters per second. Like a sprinter.
Then the band burns out. For good.
The genius.
The headlines.
The scholarship.
The offers.
Everything.
The gift. Or your best friend.
You can always get smarter.
You can't get another Leo.
You press it.
Your legs scream. The floor blurs. The air whistles above you.
12 meters. Six. Three.
You slam into Leo. You both roll.
Behind you, the screen hits the stage.
Glass, metal, dust, silence.
Then the band on your head goes cold.
The noise vanishes. The world drops back to normal. Like someone switched off a thousand lights. Tea.
Leo isn't moving. You dig into your pockets.
Candy. Sugar cubes. Always. You packed them this morning because you were always hungry.
You push one to his lips. Leo, come on, come on!
His eyelids flutter.
Medics rush in. Juice. Then fluids.
He breathes.
Your hands shake.
Dr. Lee runs up, a folder under her arm.
She looks at the broken stage. Then, at Mr.
Black, he pulls you aside.
Calm, quiet. Max, that was a freak accident. Nobody could have known.
Say that just once on the stream and I'll give you a new band. A better band.
Money, fame, a lab with your name on it.
You look at his hand, at the camera behind him. Still red, still live.
You could take it. You could be the smartest person alive.
Again, all you'd have to do is lie.
Or you could make him pay. Loud, angry, cruel.
But that fixes nothing. Truth does.
You think of Leo on the floor.
You think of 40 kids with bands on their heads.
You step to the microphone.
41 students, six hospital visits this month. A note that says, do not tell parents.
A rig built for four projectors carrying eight.
I saw the list. I wore the band too. I know what it does.
Dr. Lee lifts her folder.
The scans, the hospital records, the dates.
Nobody says a word. Hundreds of phones rise. Parents stand.
A girl in the back pulls off her band. Then a boy. Then 10 more.
They drop them on the floor one by one. Click, click, click. It sounds like rain.
Then a woman in the third row stands. Inspectors.
A father follows. Then another. Then a whole row.
Mr. Black looks for the exit.
There isn't one.
Dr. Lee puts a hand on your shoulder. You did good, kid.
You say nothing. You're shaking too hard.
By the end of the week, Lumen Labs is closed.
Remember this, a real trial never asks you to hide side effects from your doctor.

txt.s: A REAL TRIAL NEVER ASKS YOU

shots.line: Three days later, hospital room.
Leo sits up, pale, grinning, same terrible haircut.
Your mom stands at the door with a bag of sandwiches.
She hugs you so hard it hurts.
You don't have the genius anymore.
Your grades slip.
Your head is quiet, normal, slow even.
Yesterday, you walked outside and heard only birds, just birds.
You stood still and cried a little.
Nobody noticed. That was the best part.
You're not the smartest person in the room anymore. You're just a boy holding his friend's hand. It's enough.
Dr. Lee visits too.
She sits on the edge of the bed. The band took your edge, but it didn't take what you built.
The scholarship offer is still there. Slower, yes, but yours.
You nod. Slower sounds nice.
Leo squints. Hey, you came. Of course you came.
You can always get smarter. You can't get another Leo.
He frowns. Hey, how did you cross that stage so fast? Nobody runs like that.
You smile. I started early.
He rolls his eyes. Okay, okay. Listen, new joke. What did the ocean say to the beach?
You shrug. You honestly don't know.
Nothing. It just waved.
And you laugh. Right on time. The spark finally lights up.
Leo gasps. Dude, you laughed on time.
You did.
Then he taps the bed rail. Too fast, one slow.
You tap it back.
A week later, Dr. Lee calls. Max, come to the clinic.
New scan. She shows you.
Everything looks normal, except one small bright spot. It never switched off. Something in your brain is still awake.
She doesn't know why.
Neither do you.
But you remember the last thing the band did before it died. It hummed.
Like a door opening, not closing.
Then your phone buzzes. Unknown number. A single message.
We saw what you did on that stage. The band was only the beginning.
Under it, a photo, a stage, a new headband, and a date, three days from now.
So what would you do with 100 % brain?
Would you learn every language or just finally beat Leo at chess?
Tell us the first thing you'd learn in the comments. And if you'd have pressed that red switch for Leo, hit like and subscribe for part two.
